purpose: Megestrol is used to help increase appetite and promote weight gain in people who have lost a significant amount of weight due to cancer, HIV/AIDS, or other serious illnesses. It is also used to treat certain types of breast cancer and uterine cancer in women. Your doctor may prescribe it for other reasons as well.
how_it_works: Megestrol is a man-made version of a natural female hormone called progesterone. When used for appetite, it works by affecting certain chemicals in your body that control hunger, helping you feel more like eating and gain weight. When used for cancer, it helps slow the growth of certain hormone-sensitive cancer cells.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include weight gain, swelling in your hands or feet, feeling tired or weak, nausea, headache, mood changes, and decreased sex drive. Some people also notice hot flashes or vaginal bleeding. Most of these are manageable, so let your doctor know if anything bothers you.
warnings: Megestrol can increase your risk of dangerous blood clots, so tell your doctor right away if you have leg pain, swelling, chest pain, or trouble breathing. It should not be used during pregnancy as it can harm an unborn baby — use reliable birth control while taking it. People with diabetes may notice higher blood sugar levels. Long-term use can affect your adrenal glands, so do not stop taking it suddenly without talking to your doctor first.
typical_dosing: For appetite and weight loss, the usual dose is 400 to 800 mg once a day, often taken as a liquid (suspension). For cancer, doses are typically 40 to 320 mg per day divided into smaller doses. Always follow exactly what your doctor prescribes and take it at the same time each day for best results.
